subject: Hematology & ABG
title: Arterial Blood Gas Interpretation: A Stepwise Acid–Base Method
preview: Start with pH, identify the primary disturbance, check expected compensation and avoid missing a mixed acid–base disorder.
body:
Step 1: Check pH (<7.35 = Acidemia, >7.45 = Alkalemia).
Step 2: Check Primary Driver (pCO2 vs HCO3). If pH and pCO2 move in opposite directions, it is Respiratory; if same direction, Metabolic.

Step 3: Anion Gap (for Metabolic Acidosis):
Serum AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3). Normal = 12 ± 2 mEq/L.
High AG Acidosis Causes (GOLDMARK): Glycols, Oxoproline, L-lactate, D-lactate, Methanol, Aspirin, Renal failure, Ketoacidosis.

Step 4: Compensation (Winter's Formula):
Expected pCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3) + 8 ± 2.
• Measured pCO2 > Expected = Concurrent Respiratory Acidosis.
• Measured pCO2 < Expected = Concurrent Respiratory Alkalosis.

Delta Ratio (ΔAG / ΔHCO3):
• <0.4: Pure Normal AG Metabolic Acidosis.
• 0.4 - 0.8: Mixed High AG and Normal AG Acidosis.
• 1 - 2: Pure High AG Acidosis (classic DKA).
• >2: High AG Acidosis + concurrent Metabolic Alkalosis.

sections.title: Read the pH and paired values
points: Read arterial pH, PaCO₂ and bicarbonate together; avoid interpreting isolated values.
As a commonly taught adult reference interval, arterial pH is approximately 7.35–7.45, but laboratory methods and patient context matter.
A pH near normal does not exclude a mixed acid–base disorder.

sections.title: Identify the primary process
points: Acidemia with low bicarbonate points toward a metabolic acidosis; acidemia with high PaCO₂ suggests respiratory acidosis.
Alkalemia with high bicarbonate suggests metabolic alkalosis; alkalemia with low PaCO₂ suggests respiratory alkalosis.
Clinical history and measured serum chemistry results are essential.

sections.title: Compensation: ask whether it fits
points: Compensatory changes are predictable only within approximate physiologic ranges.
In metabolic acidosis, Winter’s formula estimates expected PaCO₂: 1.5 × serum HCO₃⁻ + 8 (± 2 mmHg).
Measured PaCO₂ outside the expected range suggests an additional respiratory disorder.

sections.title: Examine the anion gap
points: For metabolic acidosis, calculate anion gap using sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate) in consistent units.
Interpret anion gap with albumin concentration, electrolyte measurement technique and clinical context.

sections.title: Memory aid
points: ABG order: pH first → primary respiratory/metabolic process → expected compensation → anion gap when indicated.
Check oxygenation and the whole clinical picture separately.

sections.title: Exam trap: one value does not tell the whole story
points: Compensation alone rarely explains pH overcorrection across normal.
Multiple acid–base disturbances can coexist, especially in critically ill patients.

quiz.question: In metabolic acidosis, Winter’s formula primarily predicts which value?
A patient with metabolic acidosis has a PaCO₂ much higher than Winter’s expected value. What does this suggest?
quiz.explanation: Higher-than-expected PaCO₂ suggests an additional respiratory acidosis.

quiz.question: What is the correct first principle when interpreting an ABG?
options: Consider pH, PaCO₂ and bicarbonate together
Exclude mixed disorders when pH is near normal
quiz.explanation: Acid–base interpretation integrates all values, not a single number.
